newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serb party picks moderate leader to relief of UN.
newsitem.headline: Serb party picks moderate leader to relief of UN.

text.p: A new party formed to represent Serbs in elections in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia chose a moderate as its leader on Monday, sidelining nationalists who oppose the region's pending return to Croatian government rule.

U.N. observers at the meeting of the Independent Democratic Serb Party (SDSS) said Vojislav Stanimirovic defeated Goran Hadzic in a 19-14 vote of its executive board held in the Serb enclave's main town Vukovar.

The United Nations Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES) was relieved that Stanimirovic, who has helped negotiate accords to smooth the enclave's reintegration with Croatia, had beaten the ultra-nationalist Hadzic.

"Western observers are satisfied with the victory of a sensible man who has been negotiating with the Croatians. He has demonstrated leadership qualities in understanding the best interests of his people," said one U.N. official.

"It was striking that a small group of hardliners led by Hadzic who seemed to be slowing down if not preventing the process of registering Serbs as Croatian citizens were beaten in a vote of their peers," he told Reuters.

Four hardline members of the executive board including Hadzic then resigned in protest over a requirement for SDSS leaders to obtain Croatian citizenship to register the party for the April 13 regional elections, U.N. sources said.

Stanimirovic's takeover of the fledgling SDSS came a few days after local Serb leaders received guidance from the former patron of their 1991 separatist rebellion, Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, in a meeting in Belgrade.
U.N. sources said Milosevic advised them not to flee the region as some diehard separatists advocate, get Serbs to obtain Croatian citizenship documents and register to vote.

Serb leaders then scrapped a plan to have their people vote in a referendum for a unified county which Croatian and U.N. authorities had rejected as a last-ditch ploy to preserve Serb autonomy and keep out Croats.
The Croatian government has already promised the East Slavonian Serbs wide-ranging minority rights.
U.N. sources said Zagreb had also agreed to redraw seven of several dozen municipal districts at the Serbs' request to help them gain local majorities in the elections.

Minority Serbs seized Eastern Slavonia and two other enclaves in western Croatia in a 1991 revolt against independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia. Eastern Slavonia's majority Croat community was driven out.

Croatian troops retook the two western enclaves in 1995 attacks over U.N. truce lines, but Western diplomacy created a U.N. regime in Eastern Slavonia to prevent another war there that would have endangered the new peace in Bosnia.

Philip Arnold, UNTAES' chief spokesman, said more than 80,000 of the 120,000-odd Serbs in Eastern Slavonia had obtained Croatian citizenship papers in a sign of growing willingness to stay and accept reintegration.

UNTAES has estimated that about 15-20 percent of the region's Serbs are separatist diehards, a few of them wanted war criminals, who will flee across the nearby Danube River to Serbia before reintegration is complete this summer.
"Hundreds of Serb households have left for Serbia in recent weeks but it's only a trickle, not an exodus. The outflow is down from its peak in mid-February," said Arnold.
Croatian administrative, security and economic institutions will be phased in after the elections and almost all of 80,000 former Croat residents are expected to move back in again.
